title: Kestrel Logistics - Postmortem & Reliability Follow-up
summary: Follow-up postmortem to review last week's production incident that caused elevated 95th pct latency and a partial outage of the inference pool. We covered root cause (KV cache evictions + autoscaler race), mitigations (hotfix configuration + fallback policy), and reliability improvements (observability, canary traffic, autoscaler throttling). Agreed on a short pilot of the proposed autoscaler change and a deeper KV cache stress test.
topics: Root cause: KV cache eviction + autoscaler race

Kestrel: provide production QPS/seqlen distribution for week of incident by 2027-03-25

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-22
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Luis Ramirez (Kestrel CTO), Aisha Khan (Kestrel SRE), Ben Otieno (Kestrel PM)

Summary: quick follow-up to the incident on 2027-03-16 where the inference pool hit sustained high tail latency and partial rejection. Go over RCA, what we did, and next steps.

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this tight, uh we scheduled 45 minutes to walk through the postmortem findings and actions. Ethan's got the timeline and the root cause details, I'll kick off and then hand off.

[00:18] Ethan Cole: Cool thanks Maya. So quick TLDR: two concurrent factors, one KV cache hotset eviction during a traffic spike which surfaced because of a slightly smaller cache window after the last deploy, and second the autoscaler hit a race where scale-up decisions lagged due to the scaling controller sampling intervals, so requests started queuing, latency spiked, and some requests were rejected by the load balancer, I think that's basically it.

[00:45] Luis Ramirez: Right and from our side we saw the 95th go from 120ms to like 2.3s and error rate increase for about 18 minutes. We also had a webhook fanout that amplified the traffic a bit, that was our bad for not throttling.

[01:10] Aisha Khan: And the KV cache eviction, that - the sequence where the KV miss causes long decode path, I saw a lot of evictted keys in the log, it was pretty noisy, we still don't have full clarity if it was memory pressure or compaction.

[01:36] Ethan Cole: There is a bit of transcription/term noise in logs, but we've got snippets. The initial root cause we flagged is that the new quantization profile reduced the working set, combined with a binpacking change in the serving config, so under high seq-length variance the hot prefixes were evicted.

[02:05] Ben Otieno: Sorry quick question - was this tied to the dedicated nodes or our hosted pool? I thought we were on a dedicated cluster for the main inference path.

[02:20] Maya Patel: Good point - you're on a Dedicated capacity config but the incident affected the dedicated pool because the autoscaler for the dedicated pool didn't spin up fast enough due to sampling interval/tuning and the fallback to the hosted replica set was misconfigured - so we did see cross-pool failover attempts.

[02:50] Luis Ramirez: Right that explains why some requests were routed to a lower tier and then hit errors.

[03:05] Ethan Cole: On mitigations we pushed three things in near real-time: 1) increased the KV cache size by bumping cache_window param, 2) temporarily disabled the recent binpacking change so working sets stayed stable, 3) adjusted autoscaler sampling to be more aggressive for CPU/mem metrics and enabled a short-lived warm pool so scale-ups have capacity. That brought 95th back under acceptable thresholds in about 9 minutes after changes.

[03:40] Aisha Khan: Yeah we verified latency dropped, but we're worried about recurrence if traffic patterns change.

[03:55] Ethan Cole: Totally, long-term fixes we propose: improved cache monitoring and alerting (track hot-prefix churn, evict rate), an autoscaler throttling guard so we don't have racey double-scaling decisions, canary config rollouts for serving runtime changes, and a fallback policy that prefers local throttling instead of cross-pool failover for short windows.

[04:30] Luis Ramirez: Can you elaborate on the autoscaler throttling guard?

[04:40] Ethan Cole: Sure, it's basically a small state machine - if a scale-up was triggered in past X seconds then subsequent triggers are queued and evaluated after a short cooldown, prevents oscillation and race windows with the scheduler. Also we can add a short warm pool of pre-warmed replicas for spikes.

[05:05] Ben Otieno: For the warm pool, what's the cost impact? We need order of magnitude numbers.

[05:15] Maya Patel: Good question. Rough ballpark - a warm pool sized for your 99th percentile spike would be about 1.5-2% of steady-state cost, we can provide an exact estimate after Ethan runs a simulated workload with your QPS/seqlen distribution.

[05:38] Aisha Khan: We'll share the histograms but we also want to test the KV cache under synthetic hot-prefix churn.

[05:48] Ethan Cole: We'll run a KV-cache stress test and share results; it's part of the action items. We'll also provide the timeline doc and log snippets.

[06:05] Luis Ramirez: On the user-impact side - will Redwood offer credits? Our SRE asked about SLA credits - also need a formal postmortem doc for execs.

[06:20] Maya Patel: Yes, we'll do the formal postmortem deck and Maya will run the credits calc with the ops team, we'll share the estimate.

[06:30] Ben Otieno: Also curious - any callouts about our on-prem connectors? No, not relevant for this event.

[06:40] Ethan Cole: One other detail: we observed a bunch of per-request KV miss penalties because the KV lookups were serialized on a single thread in that path - we have an optimization that parallelizes KV lookups under certain seq-len shapes; we can evaluate enabling that, but it may increase memory use.

[07:10] Aisha Khan: We need to weigh memory vs latency tradeoff; we'll want the tests.

[07:20] Maya Patel: Recap then: Redwood to share log snippets and formal timeline by 3/24, Ethan to run KV stress tests by 3/26, Kestrel to share traffic histograms by 3/25, and we'll plan a canary pilot week of 3/29. Any objections?

[07:40] Luis Ramirez: Sounds good. Also please include the change that disabled the binpacking tweak in the timeline so our change control team can close the loop.

[08:00] Maya Patel: Absolutely. I will add the config ID and the rollback in the postmortem deck.

[08:15] Ben Otieno: On the fallback policy, I want to confirm that if the dedicated pool is degraded we prefer local throttling instead of sending to hosted - is that the plan?

[08:28] Ethan Cole: Yes, default policy will be local throttling for short windows, and cross-pool failover only after X minutes or if local capacity is exhausted and error budget allows it. We'll put knobs on that.

[08:45] Aisha Khan: One more ops ask - can we get more granular observability on per-prefix cache churn? Current dashboards are a bit coarse.

[08:56] Maya Patel: We'll add a new dashboard early next week as part of the postmortem follow-up.

[09:10] Luis Ramirez: Alright, thanks — wrap up and next steps.

[09:20] Maya Patel: Okay we'll send a follow-up email with the deck, logs, and credit calc. I'll assign owners in the doc. Meeting adjourned.

[09:30] (End of recording)

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-attributed speakers and some technical terms (binpack, KV cache) rendered inconsistently, e.g., "evictted" or "cache window" spelled inconsistently. This transcript is an export from Fireflies with timestamps every ~30-90s and contains normal speech artifacts and filler words.
notes: Real-time mitigations restored service in ~9 minutes after config changes.
Root causes: KV cache evictions (working set change after quant profile + binpacking tweak) and autoscaler race/lag.
Immediate actions: cache_window bump, rollback binpacking change, temporarily aggressive autoscaler sampling + warm pool.
Longer term: autoscaler throttling guard, canary rollouts, enhanced cache observability, simulated KV stress tests.
